title: Karan Johar Watched It at 1:35 AM and Couldn't Sleep. Raakh Is the Most Devastating Thing on Prime Video Right Now.
excerpt: Ali Fazal sheds the macho-cop swagger, Sonali Bendre returns as a grieving mother, and a 1978 wound India never healed gets reopened across eight unflinching episodes — streaming worldwide now.
body:
It was 1:35 in the morning, and Karan Johar — the man who unfollowed nearly all of Instagram days earlier to escape his screens — was back online, shaken, because he had to tell someone.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=RdB_TgwLPqs
It's 1.35 am and I am deeply disturbed after watching the last episode… Disturbed as a parent, as a human being, and as a member of society. — Karan Johar

That is the kind of word-of-mouth no marketing budget can buy. Raakh, the eight-episode crime drama that landed on Prime Video on June 12, isn't being talked about for its glamour. It's being talked about because it gets under your skin and refuses to leave. Johar called it "gut-wrenching," said he wasn't sure he'd "recover soon," and reserved a special line for the director: "a special chef's kiss to his undeniable craft."

**"Johar called it "gut-wrenching," said he wasn't sure he'd "recover soon," and reserved a special line for the director: "a special chef's kiss to his undeniable craft."

He is not alone."**

He is not alone. Filmfare handed the series a staggering 4.5 out of 5, calling it "a genuine horror show" that is "absolutely, devastatingly brilliant." That's the rare critical-and-emotional consensus that turns a quiet streaming drop into the show your group chat won't shut up about.

Here's the wound it presses on. Raakh is inspired by the Ranga-Billa case of August 1978 — one of the darkest chapters in Indian criminal memory. Siblings Geeta Chopra, 16, and Sanjay Chopra, 14, children of a naval officer, were abducted and murdered while heading to an All India Radio event in Delhi. The nation erupted. The killers were executed in 1982. For anyone of a certain generation in the diaspora, the names Ranga and Billa still carry a chill passed down from parents who lived through it. This series takes that history and dramatizes it without mercy.

!Karan Johar — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

And at its center is a quietly revelatory performance. Ali Fazal plays Sub-Inspector Jayprakash Jatav, and he made a deliberate choice to throw out the playbook.

With JP, I wanted to move away from that template completely… I was far more interested in exploring the vulnerability, empathy and emotional weight he carries than simply playing a figure of authority. — Ali Fazal

No chest-thumping. No slow-motion hero entry. Fazal builds JP as an introvert — tender, watchful, carrying his grief beneath the surface. It's the anti-cop cop, and in a landscape clogged with larger-than-life khaki-clad heroes, it lands like a slap of cold water. This is Fazal reminding everyone who only knew him from Mirzapur or his Hollywood detours that he is, first and last, a serious actor.

The casting masterstroke, though, is Sonali Bendre. The 90s icon — luminous, beloved, and largely absent from screens for years — returns as a schoolteacher and grieving mother trying to survive the unsurvivable. For diaspora viewers who grew up with her on magazine covers and movie posters, watching her dismantle herself in this role is its own kind of gut-punch. Aamir Bashir as the shattered father Jai delivers a scream of "Hai O Rabba" that critics say breaks the show wide open.

Directed by Prosit Roy (of Pari fame) and created, written and co-directed by Anusha Nandakumar and Sandeep Saket, Raakh trades jump-scares for dread. Filmfare described the first three episodes as building "a choke hold around your fears" with "quiet, surgical precision." The cinematography by Saumyananda Sahi soaks 1970s Delhi in amber gloom; the period detail is meticulous; and the storytelling, as Johar noted, never manipulates. It simply tightens.

A fair warning for the diaspora households where this will inevitably autoplay: this is not comfort viewing. If you're a parent, critics agree, it's an ordeal — the good kind that great art sometimes demands, but an ordeal nonetheless. The ending, by most accounts, is "more sorrowful than suspenseful."

The diaspora pitch is simple. It's on Prime Video, all eight episodes, streaming now in the US, UK, Canada and everywhere else — no theatrical wait, no regional lock. In a year crowded with glossy spy universes and ₹250-crore comedies, Raakh is the small, ferocious series that will outlast all of them in your memory. Watch it with the lights on. Then text someone, the way Karan Johar did, because you won't be able to hold it alone either.
